title: Stability of graphene-based single-atom catalysts across the first-row transition series: the interplay of coordination, composition, and metal identity
source_used: Abstract only, from Valency (PubMed record 42695769) and the Europe PMC core record. The paper is subscription-only (Europe PMC: isOpenAccess N, no PMCID). The RSC HTML and landing pages returned HTTP 403, the guessed ESI PDF URL returned 404, and arXiv has no preprint (API query: 0 results). Everything below is based on the abstract only.
key_findings: Systematic DFT study of 60 SACs: first-row transition metals in graphene monovacancies and divacancies, with and without N doping, plus Ni(111)-supported versions (abstract).
Metal adsorption is split into a deformation term and an intrinsic binding term (abstract).
Divacancies give 'significantly stronger and more flexible coordination environments than monovacancies' (abstract).
'carbon coordination consistently outperforms nitrogen coordination regarding the metal-graphene bond' (abstract). No magnitude is given in the abstract.
For the later transition metals, N doping weakens binding by partly filling antibonding states (abstract).
Across the series, stability is governed mainly by how the metal d states align with the graphene Fermi level, modulated by radius-dependent geometric accommodation (abstract).
Ni(111) support strengthens anchoring in DV and weakens it in SV. Magnetization and charge transfer correlate strongly with the metal-graphene binding energies (abstract).
The abstract gives no numerical binding energies.
answers:
(1) Stability quantity: the abstract speaks of a 'metal-graphene binding energy' and splits adsorption into deformation and intrinsic binding. That wording implies a binding energy relative to the isolated (gas-phase) metal atom, not a formation energy relative to the bulk metal or the cohesive energy. Without the full text this is an inference. The exact reference states, and whether the empty vacancy is relaxed, could not be checked.

(2) Sites and metals: graphene SV and DV, each pure-C or N-doped; 60 SACs in total; first-row transition metals (Sc to Zn presumably). Which N counts were used (e.g. MN3 in SV, MN4 in DV, mixed NxC) is not in the abstract and could not be checked.

(3) 'C beats N': per the abstract, a metal coordinated by C binds more strongly to the graphene than one coordinated by N ('consistently'). For the later transition metals this is attributed to N doping partly filling antibonding states. So yes: a pure-C vacancy binds the metal more strongly than the N-doped one, as a binding energy. The size of the effect is not in the abstract.

(4) Values for Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn: not available, because the full text and ESI could not be reached.

(5) S or O donors: none mentioned; only C and N, plus a Ni(111) substrate. Kinetics (diffusion or escape barriers) and dissolution potentials or Pourbaix analysis: none mentioned in the abstract.

(6) Our 'N holds better than S' and 'N, C hold better than S, O': no conflict. They do not study S or O. Our DFT E_f is relative to bulk metal with a relaxed empty doped vacancy, so it includes the cohesive energy. A binding energy relative to the free atom would rank sites differently across metals, but not between donor sets for the same metal.

One possible tension: if they find pure-C better than N-doped for Fe to Zn, that sits alongside our xTB result that N2C2, N3C or N4 in a DV are the strongest sites. Within one metal both reference choices give the same ordering, so a real comparison needs their per-metal numbers. Their C > N finding is consistent with our xTB statement that C and N both hold better than S and O. It is not consistent with any claim from us that N holds better than C. We do not make that claim; we only compare N with S.

(7) Pre-emption: it covers the systematic 'vacancy type x N/C composition x first-row metal' stability trend for graphene SACs, including DV > SV, which partly pre-empts our generic xTB conclusions (DV > SV, donor identity matters). It does not pre-empt the PDB-derived enzyme first shells, S and O donors, kinetics or NEB, dissolution potentials (U_diss), or the enzyme-to-support geometry comparison.
comparison_note: Abstract-based. The quantities differ: they report a metal-graphene binding energy (apparently relative to the isolated metal atom, split into deformation and intrinsic parts). Our DFT stability is E_f relative to bulk metal with the relaxed empty doped vacancy, and our xTB E_ins is relative to the unrelaxed or empty site. Binding energies relative to the free atom are larger in magnitude by roughly the cohesive energy, and their ranking across metals differs from E_f. For a fixed metal, donor-set rankings should agree if the empty-vacancy reference is treated the same way. Their sites are pure-C and N-doped SV and DV only; ours include S and O donors and enzyme-derived mixed sets, so the donor comparisons overlap only for C versus N. Their qualitative findings (DV stronger than SV; C at least as good as N) agree with our xTB trends (DV holds better; N and C hold better than S and O). Without their numbers we cannot check whether their C > N size matches our N4, N3C and N2C2 ordering in the DV for each metal.
impact_on_our_claims: Cite it as the closest systematic prior DFT screen of first-row TM SACs in pristine and N-doped graphene SV and DV. State that they found DV > SV and C > N coordination (binding energy relative to the free atom, presumably), and that our DV > SV finding agrees. Change our novelty wording: the general vacancy-type and donor-composition stability trend for Sc to Zn in graphene is not new. Our novelty is the PDB-derived enzyme first shells, S and O donors, a bulk-referenced E_f together with U_diss, escape and NEB kinetics, and the enzyme-to-SAC geometry transfer. In the text, state our reference energy explicitly (bulk metal, relaxed empty doped vacancy). Note that rankings relative to the free atom across metals are not comparable with E_f; our 'E_f follows the bulk cohesive energy' is partly an effect of the reference. Do not phrase our result as 'N holds better than C'. Before quoting any of their numbers, get the full text through the FU library (the RSC subscription) and check: the reference for E_b, the N count per site, and the Fe-Zn values.

title: Reactivity Screening of Single Atoms on Modified Graphene Surface: From Formation and Scaling Relations to Catalytic Activity (Jovanović, Mentus, Skorodumova, Pašti; Adv. Mater. Interfaces 2021, 2001814)
source_used: arXiv 2101.02922 PDF (author pre-peer-review version, CC BY-NC-ND), text extracted with pdftotext. Main text plus the SI bundled in the arXiv PDF (Table S1). Read: Methods Eq. 1-4, Table 1, Section 3.1 (Fig. 5 caption, Fig. 7), Table S1, Conclusions, refs [24] and [33]. The final Wiley version was not read.
key_findings: Setup: QE, PBE with ultrasoft PPs, Grimme D2 (some runs also without D2), 490 eV cutoff, spin-polarised, 4x4 graphene supercell (32 atoms), 15 Å vacuum, 4x4x1 k-mesh.

Metals: Ni, Cu, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, Ir, Pt, Au. Supports: pristine graphene; B- and N-doped graphene (C31X, substitutional, no vacancy, i.e. graphitic/quaternary N); pure-carbon single vacancy VG. No N-, S- or O-decorated vacancy and no double vacancy.
The empty VG carries a magnetic moment of 1.74 μB (dangling bonds). Vacancy formation energy is 7.76 eV.

Eq. 3: Eads(M) = E(M@G) - E(G) - E(M). E(G) is the total energy of the corresponding clean surface (with all atoms relaxed during optimisation). E(M) is the isolated metal atom, so this is an atom-referenced adsorption energy.

Aggregation criterion: Eads(M) is compared with the cohesive energy of the bulk metal. The cohesive energies are experimental values from Kittel (ref. 33), not DFT bulk energies. Fig. 5 caption: systems in the shaded region 'should not show a tendency towards aggregation'. Text: only a few M@VG systems bind strongly enough to overcome the cohesive energy.

Mobility: every metal needs at least 1 eV to leave the vacancy site. This is read from Eads heatmaps over the 25 sites, not from NEB. On BDG the value is at least 0.5 eV. NDG has a smooth landscape and is judged not a suitable support.

Dissolution: for Mz+ + support + ze- -> M@support, they take the standard potential of Mz+/M(s) and correct it by the difference between Eads(M) and the bulk cohesive energy (method from their ref. 24, Johansson et al. PCCP 2017). Stability is then judged against the water window for pH 0-14.

Table S1, E°(Mz+/M@VG) vs SHE: Ni (z=2, E°bulk -0.25) +0.92 V; Cu (z=2, 0.337) +0.54 V; Ru (z=3, 0.6) +1.24 V; Pt (z=2, 1.188) +1.97 V. For NDG: Ni -1.63, Cu -1.04, Ru -0.88, Pt -0.54 V. Ag@VG is -0.11 V. Ir has no data.
Conclusion: Ru, Rh, Pd and Pt on VG should never dissolve over pH 0-14; Ni and Cu on VG are stable at high pH. Pristine, NDG and BDG dissolve more easily than the bulk metals.
answers:
(1) Definition. Eads(M) = E(M@support) - E(clean support) - E(isolated M atom). Stability against aggregation means |Eads| exceeds the bulk cohesive energy, so in effect Eads + Ecoh < 0. Ecoh is the experimental value from Kittel; the paper uses no DFT bulk reference. Their quantity is therefore the same kind as our E_f (metal in site vs. empty relaxed site vs. bulk metal), but they mix a DFT free-atom reference with an experimental Ecoh. We use a consistent DFT bulk energy.

(2) Supports: pristine, substitutional B- and N-doped graphene (no vacancy), and a pure-carbon single vacancy. Metals: Ni, Cu, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, Ir, Pt, Au.

(3) Single-vacancy numbers, PBE / PBE+D2: Ni -6.52/-6.78, Cu -3.63/-3.89, Ru -8.30/-8.66, Pt -6.91/-7.41 eV. Dissolution potentials on VG: Ni +0.92, Cu +0.54, Ru +1.24, Pt +1.97 V vs SHE.

My own back-calculation (not stated in the paper) uses Kittel Ecoh (Ni 4.44, Cu 3.49, Ru 6.74, Pt 5.84 eV) in E° = E°bulk - (Eads + Ecoh)/z. It reproduces all four Table S1 values exactly with the PBE+D2 Eads, so the implied E_f vs bulk is about Ni -2.34, Cu -0.40, Ru -1.92, Pt -1.57 eV. These four Ecoh values are not printed in the text I read; please check them against Kittel.

(4) Why they find SV stable and we do not. This is mainly a real chemical difference in the site, not a definitional conflict.
- Their VG is a pure-carbon vacancy with three dangling bonds (1.74 μB). Our Cu-N3 and Ni-N3 SV sites are pyridinic-N-terminated vacancies whose empty reference is already saturated. Both works use the relaxed empty site as reference, so the reference definition is the same.
- Their "N-doped" support is graphitic N without a vacancy, which is a different system again. On it they find aggregation is favoured, and the dissolution potentials are strongly negative.
- Even on the pure-C SV, Cu is only marginally stable (about -0.40 eV implied), so our Cu-N3 at +0.68 eV is about 1 eV less favourable. The direction matches our own trend of more C donors binding the metal more strongly: Cu-N3 +0.68, Cu-N2C about +0.45 (from U_diss +0.11), then their C3 at about -0.40.
- Secondary differences, which I estimate are smaller than the site chemistry (an assessment, not in the paper): D2 vs D3(BJ) (D2 adds 0.26-0.50 eV to Eads on VG for these metals), PBE free-atom vs experimental Ecoh mixing, 4x4 vs 6x6 cell, and their reading of Fig. 5 vs Table S1.

(5) Dissolution. Their criterion has the same Greeley-Nørskov form as our U_diss = U0 - E_f/n. They then test it against the HER/OER window over pH 0-14. Our numbers (Co-N2OC +0.51 V, Cu-N2C +0.11 V) are directly comparable to their Cu@VG +0.54 V and Ni@VG +0.92 V.
comparison_note:
The definition is the same in spirit: metal in the relaxed site vs. the relaxed empty site vs. the bulk metal, with U = U0 - E/n. The differences are in the sites and references:
(a) Their single vacancy is pure carbon with dangling bonds. Our SV sites are N/S/O-terminated, and none of their supports is a heteroatom-decorated vacancy.
(b) Their "N-doped graphene" is graphitic N without a vacancy, not our pyridinic N3 vacancy.
(c) Their bulk reference is the experimental Kittel cohesive energy combined with a DFT isolated-atom energy (PBE+D2, ultrasoft, 4x4 cell). Ours is a DFT bulk energy (PBE-D3(BJ), GBRV, 6x6 cell).
Their implied E_f for Cu@VG (about -0.40 eV, back-calculated from Table S1) and our Cu-N3 (+0.68) and Cu-N2C (about +0.45) follow one trend: replacing N donors by C lowers E_f. So there is no conflict. Their kinetic statement (at least 1 eV to leave the vacancy, from adsorption heatmaps) is cruder than our escape + NEB analysis but consistent with it.
impact_on_our_claims:
1. Add a sentence to the report: E_f > 0 for N3- or S-terminated SV sites does not contradict Jovanović et al. Their stable M@VG sites are pure-carbon vacancies with dangling bonds (Cu@VG only marginally stable), and their substitutional N-doped graphene is unstable to aggregation and dissolution.
2. Cite their dissolution potentials as a benchmark for our U_diss. Their M@VG values vs SHE are Ni +0.92, Cu +0.54, Ru +1.24 and Pt +1.97 V, from the same E° - (Eads + Ecoh)/z construction. Our Cu-N2C at +0.11 V sits between Cu-N3 (about 0 V) and their Cu@C3 (+0.54 V).
3. Recommended check: run Cu and Ni in a pure-C3 single vacancy with our setup (D3(BJ), 6x6, DFT bulk reference). If we get about -0.4 / -2.3 eV, the difference is confirmed as site chemistry and not method.
4. Present "C donors hold the metal more strongly than N" as consistent with this paper. Note that our "N holds better than S" conclusion is not tested by them.
5. The approach claim (PDB-derived first shells) is unaffected, since they screen generic supports only.

title: Tuning the metal-support interactions in transition metal-anchored heteroatom-doped graphene single-atom catalysts (van Dam & Vermeeren, PCCP 2026, 28(27):16366-16381)
source_used: PubMed Central full text (PMC13248922, via PubMed; https://doi.org/10.1039/d6cp00932h). The PMC JSON text has citation markers stripped, so I read the reference list from the PMC web page (WebFetch, two passes). I matched author names in the text to reference numbers by surname and topic. These matches are my inference, not stated links. No SI was needed: this is a review and has no own data tables.
key_findings: Qualitative review with no own calculations. The main text gives no binding or formation energy values for any cited study; the only numbers are geometric (e.g. N-doped DV: Sc, Ti, V lifted 1.0-1.3 A; B-doped DV: all TMs displaced 1.0-1.6 A; Ti-4NDG and Ba-4NDG elevations 0.89 and 1.72 A; ~0.1 A TM-C bond shortening from Mn to Zn in TM-3CDG).

Vacancy type: majority view is DV > SV (Di Valentin, Koskinen, Gao, Soldano, Kim). The planar DV gives better orbital overlap; in SV the metal sits out of plane (trigonal pyramidal). Dai (Fe) and Zheng (Sc-Zn, Pd, Pt) report SV > DV. The review traces this to the reference choice: those energies include the relaxation and deformation of the bare vacancy, and the reconstructed 5-8-5 DV is a stable reference.
Doping at SV: any doping (N, B, N/B) weakens binding relative to undoped 3C (Dai, Gaudry, Kim, Gao, Mavrikakis, Yan, Zheng). Kim's ordering puts 3N (SV) last.

Doping at DV: N generally strengthens binding. Kim's order of N motifs (SV and DV together): (5-ring)/(6-ring)-type 2N2C > 3N1C ~ (5-ring)-2N2C ~ 1N3C > (6-ring)-2N2C > 4C ~ 4N ~ 3C > 2N1C, 1N2C > 3N. Mavrikakis: partially doped TM-3N1C DV binds most strongly.

Zhang (Fe-4XDG, N/O/C mixtures): more N strengthens Fe-NxO(4-x); Fe-C and Fe-N bonds are of comparable strength in Fe-NxC(4-x); more O lowers binding in Fe-OxC(4-x). Conclusion: N and C anchor Fe well, O destabilises.

Kulik (Fe-4XDG molecular flakes, X = N, O, P, S): Fe-support bonding is strongest for N, then P, then S, then O. P and S distort the support out of plane; forcing them planar shortens the bonds and weakens binding.

Pasti (Mn, Fe, Co; TM-OxNy and TM-SxNy, x+y = 4, DV): replacing N in TM-4N by O or S destabilises the site (bonding energies plus Pourbaix). At low N content, bonding energies are less favourable than the metal cohesive energy, so these sites are prone to demetallation.
Zhao (TM = Sc-Zn, X = B, N, O, P, S, all DV): period-3 dopants (P, S) always cause out-of-plane distortion. Dopants with a radius close to C are favoured for structural integrity.
Tang (periods 4-6, X = B, N, O, P, S, DV): O doping lowers thermodynamic stability, more O lowers it further, and undoped TM-4C shows the best structural stability.

Overall conclusion of the review: N in DV (cis-2N2C preferred) is the best anchor. Period-2 dopants (B, O) weaken binding less than period-3 dopants (P, S). No SV study with S or O donors is discussed.

Metal trend: Fe, Co and Ni bind 4N most strongly (van Dam & Vermeeren, Chem. Eur. J. 2025: 3d(x2-y2)-N lone-pair HOMO-LUMO picture); Cu and Zn are weakest. In TM-3C, Ti is often the strongest. The review says reported trends are fragmented and partly contradictory, and calls for reporting of coordinates, spin states and oxidation states.
answers:
(1) The review does not scan S, O and C donors itself. It cites systematic donor scans, all for DV only:
- Zhao, ref 40: Sc-Zn with B, N, O, P, S; structural.
- Tang, ref 41: periods 4-6 with B, N, O, P, S.
- Pasti, ref 38: Mn, Fe, Co with OxNy and SxNy.
- Kulik, ref 39: Fe with N, O, P, S, using flakes.
- Zhang, ref 36: Fe with NxOy, NxCy, OxCy.
- Yang, ref 56: N,S co-doped DV, Sc-Hg, with dissolution potentials.
No cited work covers S or O donors in SV sites, and none has mixed S/C or N/S/C first shells like our Cu-N2S or Fe-NS2 SV sites.

(2) Trends:
- DV binds more strongly than SV (majority view). SV > DV appears only when the energy is taken against the relaxed or reconstructed empty vacancy (Dai, Zheng).
- Any doping weakens SV sites. N strengthens DV sites, and partial N (2N2C, 3N1C) is strongest.
- For Fe-DV, N and C are about equal and O weakens (Zhang).
- Kulik ranks N > P > S > O for Fe-DV.
- Pasti: O or S in place of N destabilises the site.
- Tang: more O lowers stability, and undoped 4C is structurally best.
- Period-3 dopants (P, S) distort the site.

(3) There is no enzyme-, metalloprotein-, PDB- or bio-inspired SAC design anywhere in the text, and no stability dataset like ours that combines E_f, U_diss, escape barriers and NEB over many N/S/O/C first shells. The closest are Tang (DV, B/N/O/P/S, periods 4-6), Zhao, Kim (N-doping SV/DV, periods 4-6) and Yang (N,S DV, dissolution potentials).

(4) Most relevant cited works for N vs S vs O vs C:
- Jia...Kulik, J. Mater. Chem. A 2022, 10, 6193 (ref 39)
- Ritopecki...Pasti, Nanomaterials 2022, 12, 4309 (ref 38)
- Han...Zhang H., PCCP 2022, 24, 18854 (ref 36)
- Gallagher...Zhao Q., PCCP 2025, 27, 5464 (ref 40)
- Huang...Tang Q., Chem. Commun. 2026, 62, 3338 (ref 41)
- Liu...Yang L.-M., Fuel 2026, 417, 138650 (ref 56)
- Ha...Kim K. S., Energy Environ. Sci. 2021, 14, 3455 (ref 23)
- Kropp...Mavrikakis, Catal. Sci. Technol. 2019, 9, 6793 (ref 31)
- Zhang X....Zheng W., RSC Adv. 2015, 5, 82804 (ref 25)
- Dobrota...Pasti, Electrochim. Acta 2022, 412, 140155 (ref 54)
- Di Liberto...Pacchioni, ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 45 (ref 13)
comparison_note:
Where we agree:
- N holds the metal better than S, and S and O are weaker than N and C. This matches Kulik (N > P > S > O), Pasti (O or S in place of N destabilises), Zhang (Fe-N about equal to Fe-C; O weakens) and Tang (O destabilises).
- DV > SV, and the strongest sites being N2C2, N3C or N4 in a DV, match Kim and Mavrikakis (partial N such as 2N2C or 3N1C is best).

Where we differ:
- The review's S-vs-O order for Fe-DV is S > O (Kulik). We only say both are weaker than N and C, so check whether our xTB per-metal coefficients rank S vs O the same way.
- The review says Tang finds undoped 4C structurally best. That differs from our N4 or N2C2 being best, but it is close to our N/C equivalence.

Definitions:
- Most cited works use a binding energy relative to the isolated gas-phase atom, often against the frozen or relaxed vacancy. Our E_f uses the relaxed empty doped vacancy and bulk metal per atom, so it includes the cohesive energy. That explains why we see "E_f follows bulk cohesive energy" and positive E_f for most sites, while the literature reports large negative binding energies.
- Our E_ins (xTB) and E_f both take the relaxed empty site as reference. That is the 'deformation-included' framework the review links to the Dai and Zheng SV > DV results. Our DV > SV is therefore not an artefact of an intrinsic-interaction definition.
- Pasti also compares bonding energies with metal cohesion energies, which is conceptually closest to our E_f > 0 criterion.

Scope: the review gives no numbers, so no value-level comparison is possible.
impact_on_our_claims:
1. Cite this review as the current summary of donor and vacancy trends. Add the S/O/C donor scans it cites as prior work on the donor ordering: Kulik ref 39, Pasti refs 38 and 54, Zhang ref 36, Zhao ref 40, Tang ref 41, Yang ref 56, plus Kim ref 23 and Mavrikakis ref 31 for N motifs and SV vs DV.
2. Narrow the novelty claim. Systematic B/N/O/P/S DV scans across periods 4-6 already exist (Tang, Zhao). Our novelty is (a) enzyme/PDB-derived first shells, which the review shows are absent, (b) mixed N/S/O/C shells in SV sites, which no cited work covers, and (c) the combined thermodynamic and kinetic screen (E_f, U_diss, escape energy, NEB).
3. State our reference energies explicitly: relaxed empty doped vacancy plus bulk metal. Note that this includes vacancy deformation, the framework the review links to SV > DV reversals in Dai and Zheng. Our E_f is not directly comparable with gas-phase-atom binding energies.
4. Compare our S-vs-O ordering with Kulik's N > P > S > O (Fe-DV, flakes) and Zhao's finding that period-3 dopants always distort the site; our S sites in SV may show the same distortion.
5. Our 'E_f follows bulk cohesive energy' can be linked to Pasti's observation that low-N sites have bonding energies below the metal cohesive energy.

title: Role of heteroatom-doping in enhancing catalytic activities and the stability of single-atom catalysts for oxygen reduction and oxygen evolution reactions (Zheng, Han, Wang, Xia; Nanoscale 2022, 14(43), 16286-16294)
source_used: Abstract only, from the Valency/PubMed record (PMID 36301010) and the Semantic Scholar API. The paper has no PMCID. The RSC article HTML and landing pages returned HTTP 403. Semantic Scholar reports isOpenAccess=false with no OA PDF. OSTI has no record, and the Unpaywall query failed (HTTP 422). We could not read the main text or the SI.
key_findings: The abstract names only S as the dopant: 'S-doped transition metal-nitrogen-carbon SAC structures'. It does not mention O, P or B doping (abstract-based).

Host: M-N-C single-atom sites, by the abstract's wording. The abstract does not give the exact coordination (e.g. M-N4 to M-N3S or M-N2S2), whether S sits in the first or second shell, or which metals were studied.

The abstract says stability, electronic structure and ORR/OER overpotentials were computed with first-principles methods. It does not state the stability metric (formation energy, binding vs cohesive energy, dissolution potential) or any numbers.
The abstract frames doping as a way to get 'highly efficient and stable SACs', which implies the authors report S doping as stabilising or at least compatible with stability. No magnitude is given.
The authors propose an intrinsic descriptor that links catalyst properties to ORR/OER activity, use it for screening, and report agreement with experiment.
answers: We have the abstract only; the full text is paywalled and not in PMC. (1) Heteroatoms: the abstract mentions only S, doped into transition metal-N-C SAC sites (M-N-C, presumably M-N4-derived). title: Bioinspired Design of Heterogenous Single-Atomic-Site Catalysts for Electrocatalysis and Photocatalysis (Wang, Jia, Yang, Zhang, Wong; Adv. Mater. 2025, 37(48), e2502131)
source_used: PubMed Central full text PMC12676108 (PMID 40525774), read completely (~100k characters: all sections 1-4, Tables 1-2, figure captions). The PMC JSON text loses subscripts, so the coordination formulas were taken from two WebFetch passes over the PMC HTML page (characters 0-200,000 of 213,380; the last ~13k characters, probably references, were not read). The formulas come from the WebFetch summariser and should be spot-checked against the PDF. The article is a review and has no SI.
key_findings: Type: a narrative review with no new calculations. It is organised by design level: first shell (metal centre, coordination number, coordination species), second/long-range shell (heteroatom doping, dual-metal sites, nano-single-atom sites, metal-support interaction) and outer microenvironment (non-covalent interactions, mass/proton/electron transfer). It then covers applications by enzyme class.

Table 2 groups templates into four enzyme classes. Hydrogenase (Ni/Fe) -> Ni/Fe/Ru/Cu single atoms, HER. Nitrogenase (Fe/Mo) -> Fe/Mo/Ru single atoms, NRR/NORR. Oxidase (Fe/Cu) -> Fe/Co/Cu/Se single atoms, ORR. Dehydrogenase (Mo/W) -> Fe/Ni/Co/Cu single atoms, CO2RR.

Other enzyme templates in the text: peroxidase/heme (Fe-N4, Fe-N4O2), Cu superoxide dismutase (Cu-N4), laccase and cytochrome c oxidase (Cu, Fe-Cu), chlorophyll (Mg-N4), Mn enzymes (Mn-N3O1 on graphene), axial-His heme/hemoglobin (FeN5, FeNx with x = 4-6), square-pyramidal Ni in SOD (Ni-N5 vs planar Ni-N4), vitamin B12 (CoN4S, axial S), reductive dehalogenase (Co on BCN), ferredoxin (Fe2N6-S), CODH (Fe-Ni-N-C; Co with N,S sites in a COF), formate dehydrogenase (Cu-Se(-Zn) in ZnSe; [NiS4] dithiolene MOF), glutathione peroxidase (Se-C), sulfite oxidase (Fe in MoS2).

PDB use: entries appear only as illustrations in figures (1HCH horseradish peroxidase, Figs. 1-2; 1N2C nitrogenase; 1GYC laccase; 1SU8 CODH; 1TV8 MoaA). Neither the review nor the cited works it describes mine the PDB or any metalloprotein database (MetalPDB etc.) systematically.

Stability is treated only qualitatively (Section 4.3). SACs are 'prone to dissolution, detachment, aggregation, and poisoning'. Proposed remedies: strong metal-support interaction, spatial confinement, self-adaptive single atoms, reversible valence states. The review gives no formation energies, dissolution potentials, binding/cohesive-energy criteria or aggregation barriers. 'Formation energy' appears only in the Fig. 5b caption (ZnB2N2 vs ZnN4), without a number.

Synthesis is treated qualitatively. Top-down routes: etching, ball milling, microwave, laser. Bottom-up routes: wet chemistry, pyrolysis, defect engineering. Quantitative statements: enzyme metal content 0.05-5 wt%; SAC loading above 5 wt% is 'extremely challenging'; some reports exceed 20 wt%; minimum industrial catalyst scale about 100 kg.

Mixed or low-coordinate first shells reported as made experimentally (precedents): CuN3 SAzyme (Li et al.; fewer N 'protrude[s]' Cu out of the carbon plane vs planar CuN4); Fe-N3 with N defects (Qu); Fe-N4O2 (Shi); Mn-N3O1 on graphene (Chen, ORR / Zn-air); MnN3S1 in S,N-C (Chen, CO2RR); Fe-S1N3 (Cui, CO2RR); V-S1N3 (Li, Li-S); FeN3P; Co1-P1N3; ZnB2N2; CoN4S axial S; Ni-N4 with axial Cl/Br/I; Fe2N6-S dual Fe; Co with N,S sites in THD-COF; [NiS4] in a Ni-dithiolene MOF; Fe-S-C (Fe-SC2 in the Fig. 13d caption).

Selection of templates: chosen by hand and by literature. Each example is a separate prior study in which the authors picked one enzyme by analogy. The review proposes ML or bioinspired-ML screening only as a future opportunity (Section 4.1) and notes that 'current SACs research relies on a trial-and-error processes'.
answers:
Templates: hand-picked, enzyme-by-enzyme analogies collected from the literature. Main sources: heme peroxidase and hemoglobin, Cu-SOD, laccase and cytochrome c oxidase, chlorophyll, Mn enzymes, B12, Ni-SOD, reductive dehalogenase, ferredoxin, hydrogenase, nitrogenase, CODH, FDH, GPx and sulfite oxidase. These are grouped in Table 2 into hydrogenase, nitrogenase, oxidase and dehydrogenase. Each first shell is described in words (M-N4, axial N/S/halogen, N/S/P/B/O substitution) rather than taken from structures. There is no systematic selection.

PDB or database mining: none. PDB IDs (1HCH, 1N2C, 1GYC, 1SU8, 1TV8) appear only in figures. ML screening is named only as a future direction.

Stability and synthesis: qualitative only (dissolution, detachment, aggregation, poisoning; remedies such as SMSI and confinement). There are no E_f, U_diss or kinetic criteria. The only numbers concern loading (>5 wt% hard, >20 wt% reported, enzymes 0.05-5 wt%) and scale (about 100 kg).

Mixed-shell or low-CN experimental precedents: CuN3 (out of plane), Fe-N3, Fe-N4O2, Mn-N3O1 on graphene, MnN3S1, Fe-S1N3, V-S1N3, FeN3P, Co1-P1N3, ZnB2N2, CoN4S (axial S), Fe2N6-S, Co-N,S in a COF, [NiS4] in a MOF. None of these is an exact match for our Fe-NS2, Co-N2OC, Ni-N3 or Zn-N3. The closest analogues are CuN3 for Cu-N3, Fe-N3 and Fe-S1N3 for Fe-NS2, and Mn-N3O1 and Fe-N4O2 for O-containing shells such as Co-N2OC.
comparison_note:
This is a qualitative review with no E_f, E_ins, U_diss or barrier values, so our numbers have nothing to be checked against. The only 'formation energy' mention (ZnB2N2 called 'most stable', Fig. 5b) has no stated value or reference state, so it cannot be compared with our E_f, which is referenced to the metal-free doped vacancy plus the bulk metal.

The review gives the experimental existence of CuN3, Fe-N3, Fe-S1N3, MnN3S1 and Mn-N3O1. Our DFT gives E_f > 0 against bulk metal for Cu-N3 SV (+0.68 eV) and most S-containing sites. These two statements do not conflict: experimental SACs come from pyrolysis or wet chemistry under kinetic control, and the exact first shells in those papers come from EXAFS fitting, not from our SV/DV vacancy models.

The review's qualitative statements agree with our geometry and chemistry. CuN3 protrudes out of the carbon plane relative to planar CuN4, consistent with our SV metal sitting about 0.8 A out of plane. S has lower electronegativity and a larger radius than N and gives 'higher electron localization'. The review does not say that S holds metals more weakly.

Mater. review in which every template is hand-picked, PDB entries are only illustrations, and ML screening is a stated future need. Synthesis is kinetic, and the references differ: our E_f uses the relaxed metal-free doped vacancy plus bulk M, while experiments report EXAFS-fitted shells. This framing is also a reason to present the kinetic (escape/NEB) criterion beside E_f.
4) The review has no precedents for Fe-NS2 (two S), Co-N2OC, Ni-N3 or Zn-N3. Do not cite it as a precedent for those sites.

title: QuantumPDB: A Workflow for High-Throughput Quantum Cluster Model Generation from Protein Structures (Kastner, Luo, Ho, Reinhardt, Keys, Kulik; J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2026, 66(10), 6011-6026)
source_used: PubMed Central full text, PMC13213834 (main text only; SI not read). Valency record 42086224 for the abstract and bibliographic data.
key_findings: Purpose: an open-source Python package that turns raw PDB files into QM cluster models (Modeller rebuilds missing parts, Protoss assigns protonation, Voronoi-contact interaction spheres, TeraChem or ORCA input with optional MM point charges, Multiwfn charge and dipole analysis).

Spheres: the first sphere is set by a parameter that defaults to a 4.0 A radial distance from a user-defined center. The second and tertiary spheres are not distance-based; each is the set of residues in Voronoi contact with the previous sphere. Dummy grid atoms regularise the cells in sparse regions. Point charges are included out to 20.0 A from the cluster centroid by default (ff14SB charges, TIP3P water).

The center is user-defined and can be a metal (e.g. every Fe), several merged residues (a diiron core within 4.0 A, PHM Cu sites more than 11 A apart merged with a 12.0 A cutoff, heme+O2+His), a substrate, or an oligomer.

Metal oxidation states and spin multiplicities are not assigned automatically; the user supplies them in a CSV. Heuristics reorient His rings toward the metal, deprotonate metal-bound Cys and Tyr, and deprotonate backbone N within 3.0 A of a metal.

Showcase metal sites (figures only, no data set): MMO, PHM, oxymyoglobin, NHase, TauD, Langerin Ca. First/second-sphere atom counts are 102/613 for MMO, 46/421 for PHM, 453/1112 for MbO2 and 105/611 for NHase.

Data set: a PDB query on 6 Aug 2024 over EC classes 1-7 returned 101,633 structures. The filtering steps left 100,300 (UniProt), 61,623 (ligand-bound), 59,495 (X-ray, <3.0 A, with DOI), 57,580 (size filter) and finally 989 holo-enzymes with native substrates (Rhea/ChEBI match).

QM: 1,673 cluster models of 842 enzymes (abstract), with clusters centered on the substrate. Level of theory is omegaPBEh-D3(BJ)/LACVP* single points with GPU acceleration. Models have 132-812 QM atoms (primary + secondary spheres) plus MM point charges, compared with the substrate alone in implicit solvent (eps = 80).

Results: substrate charge moves toward neutral. The charge difference ranges from +1.5 to -3.2 (mean -0.2); 381 of 1673 (23.1 %) change by less than 0.1. The substrate dipole is consistently reduced. Charge difference and dipole difference do not correlate (r = 0.02). FNR correlates with hydropathy at 0.56.
Timings (median, serial): cluster generation 2.79 s, Modeller 7.09 s, Protoss 9.05 s.
Related-work note in the paper: molSimplify's Protein3D class 'automates extraction of the metalloenzyme primary coordination spheres' but goes no further than the first sphere.
answers: What it extracts: whole residues in contact-based interaction spheres (primary, secondary, tertiary) around a user-chosen center. The center is a metal only if the user asks for one. In the case study it is the native substrate, not a metal. It does not classify donor atoms, and it is not a PDB-wide sweep of metal sites. The worked data set is 989 holo-enzymes (from 101,633 EC-annotated PDB entries), giving 1,673 clusters of 842 enzymes. Level of theory: omegaPBEh-D3(BJ)/LACVP* single points (TeraChem), with clusters of 132-812 atoms plus ff14SB point charges. There are no geometry optimisations and no energies used as results; the reported properties are partial charges (Hirshfeld etc. via Multiwfn) and dipoles. Purpose: automated QM-cluster set-up for enzyme electrostatics and catalysis, shown on substrate charge transfer and dipole changes. It does not transfer sites to materials or catalysts and computes no stability, formation, binding or dissolution energies. Overlap with our work: automated parsing of the PDB around metal centers, metal-ligand heuristics (His orientation, Cys/Tyr deprotonation, backbone-N within 3.0 A) and the idea of high-throughput QM on enzyme sites. Differences: our sweep covers 291,977 metal sites, defines the first shell at the level of donor atoms with N/S/O/C classification, rebuilds sites in graphene vacancies and screens stability (E_f, U_diss, E_ins, escape barriers). None of this is in QuantumPDB. Citation: yes, as related work on automated PDB-to-QM-cluster pipelines, and it supports our novelty claim, since it stays entirely inside the protein. It also points to molSimplify Protein3D as an existing tool for extracting first coordination spheres, which we should check and cite. Second sphere: its Voronoi-contact secondary sphere could define the enzyme second sphere for our sites, for example (a) an enzyme reference cluster for comparing geometry and charge with our graphene models, or (b) a list of second-sphere H-bond partners to mimic with dopants or functional groups. It cannot be pasted into a periodic graphene cell. Its 'first sphere' (residues within 4.0 A of the center) is not the same as our donor-atom first shell.
comparison_note: No common quantity. QuantumPDB reports charges and dipoles from omegaPBEh-D3(BJ)/LACVP* single points on protein clusters with point-charge embedding. We report PBE-D3(BJ) plane-wave periodic energies (E_f against the doped vacancy without M plus bulk metal, U_diss, dG_H) and xTB insertion energies. Their sphere definitions differ from ours. Their 'first sphere' is a set of whole residues within a default 4.0 A of a center that may be a substrate, a metal or merged residues, and further spheres follow Voronoi contacts. Our 'first shell' means the donor atoms bonded to the metal. Their data set is 989 substrate-bound enzymes, selected for native substrates rather than for metals. Our sweep covers 291,977 metal sites PDB-wide, so the counts cannot be compared.
impact_on_our_claims: (1) Cite QuantumPDB in related work as an automated PDB-to-QM-cluster workflow (with Protein3D/molSimplify, QMzyme, RINRUS, EnzyHTP), and say clearly that it stays inside the protein: no transfer to supports, no stability screen. That supports our approach claim. (2) Check and cite molSimplify's Protein3D, which the paper says extracts metalloenzyme primary coordination spheres. That is the closest precedent for our first-shell extraction, so our novelty wording should be 'transfer to SAC models plus a stability screen', not 'first-shell extraction'. (3) Optional extension: use QuantumPDB secondary spheres (Voronoi contacts) to build enzyme reference clusters for a few showcase sites (e.g. Cu-N3, Co-N2OC). These would improve our 'vs the enzyme' geometry comparison and could guide second-sphere dopant choices. Note that it requires user-supplied oxidation and spin states. (4) Use 'first coordination shell (donor atoms)' consistently and contrast it with their residue-level 'primary interaction sphere'.

W. Kastner et al., J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2026, 66, 6011-6026, doi:10.1021/acs.jcim.5c03064).

title: Generalizable mechanochemical impact of curvature governing stability and reactivity at catalytic sites on rippled supports (Banerjee & Mandal, PCCP 2026, 28(15):9617-9626)
source_used: Valency/PubMed abstract (id 41924911). Europe PMC lists it as not open access ("Subscription required"), not in PMC. The RSC article HTML, landing and DOI-redirect pages all returned HTTP 403. No chemRxiv/arXiv preprint turned up in the Valency title search, and the chemRxiv API also returned 403. No full text or SI was read.
key_findings: Method (abstract): first-principles DFT on graphene-supported M-N-C single-atom sites with 3d, 4d and 5d transition-metal centres. Curvature is treated as a vector descriptor, i.e. both its magnitude and its sign (direction) are varied. The abstract gives no functional, cell size, curvature values or strain percentages.

Stability: 'curvature modulates the thermodynamic stability of single-atom sites, with larger metal centers being preferentially stabilized in regions of higher curvature' (qualitative; no eV values in the abstract).

H adsorption is used as the model case for bonding (covalency/ionicity). Curvature tunes the M-H bond strength, most strongly for early transition metals. The abstract does not say whether this is dE_H or dG_H, and gives no numbers.
CO2: the sign of curvature can change the activation mechanism at a given metal. Curvature enhances CO2 adsorption and activation even for metals that are inactive on flat surfaces.
General trend: early TMs respond more to curvature than late TMs.
No eV per % strain or eV per curvature (1/A) slope can be extracted. None is reported in the accessible text.
answers:
Sites/metals: M-N-C single-atom sites in graphene (most likely M-N4-type, but the abstract does not state the coordination or the vacancy type) for 3d, 4d and 5d TMs. The specific metals are not listed in the abstract.

Size of the effect: no numbers are accessible, so there is no eV/% strain or eV/curvature value. Qualitatively, curvature stabilises larger metals more, and early TMs are more sensitive than late TMs.

H adsorption: yes, H adsorption is the model case for M-H bonding vs curvature. Whether the authors report dG_H (with ZPE/entropy corrections) or a raw dE_H cannot be checked without the full text.

Flat cell under- or overestimating stability (abstract-based): the abstract implies that for larger (4d/5d) metals, curved or rippled regions are more stable than flat ones. A flat 6x6 cell would then tend to underestimate stability for those metals at curved sites, with a smaller effect for late 3d metals such as Cu, Ni, Co and Zn. The abstract does not say whether the stability measure is E_f referenced to bulk metal or a binding energy referenced to the isolated atom. It also does not say whether the curved empty vacancy is used as the reference (which would cancel part of the strain energy). The magnitude and sign for our specific metals therefore cannot be confirmed.

Conflict with our xTB result: no direct conflict. Our statement is that geometry mismatch/strain adds no predictive power within a metal on flat supports, i.e. mismatch between enzyme geometry and vacancy geometry. They vary the support's own curvature, a variable that is absent from our flat models. Their result says curvature is an extra design dimension. That is complementary, not contradictory, but it limits our claim to flat supports.
comparison_note: Different quantity and setup. They vary the curvature (sign and magnitude) of the graphene support around M-N-C sites. We use a flat 6x6 cell and define strain as the mismatch between the enzyme first-shell geometry and the vacancy. Their stability metric and reference energies are unknown from the abstract: it could be E_f vs bulk metal like our E_f, or a binding energy vs the free atom, and the curved empty site may or may not be the reference. So even the sign of 'stabilisation' cannot be mapped onto our E_f or U_diss values. Their H-adsorption quantity (dE_H vs dG_H) is also unspecified. Their metal-size trend (larger metals favoured at higher curvature) is qualitatively consistent with our SV picture, where the metal sits ~0.8 A out of plane, a local curvature-like distortion. Comparing numbers is impossible without the full text.
impact_on_our_claims: 1) In the limitations section, add that all our E_f, U_diss and dG_H values are for flat graphene. Real carbons are rippled or curved, and DFT work (Banerjee & Mandal 2026) reports that curvature changes M-N-C stability (favouring larger metals at higher curvature) and M-H bond strength (most for early TMs). Our flat values may therefore underestimate the stability of 4d/5d sites at curved regions, and dG_H for early TMs may shift. 2) State the xTB claim precisely: 'geometry mismatch between enzyme and vacancy adds no predictive power within a metal on flat supports'. Do not generalise it to 'strain does not matter'. 3) Optional: name curvature as a future descriptor (e.g. a few curved or rippled cells for Co-N2OC, Zn-N3 and Cu-N3). 4) Do not quote any number from this paper until someone with RSC access has checked the full text and SI.

title: Potential-Induced Dynamic Coordination of Nonmetal Atoms Directly Bound to Metal Centers in Graphene-Embedded Single-Atom Catalysts and Its Implications (Li, Li, Yan, Liu, Yu, Ma; arXiv v1, 4 Feb 2026, preprint without journal reference)
source_used: The arXiv HTML version returned 404. I read the full arXiv PDF (v1, 35 pages: main text plus Supporting Information Figs. S1-S9, Table S1 and Note 1) after converting it with pdftotext. Values printed inside figures (heat map in Fig. 2a, Fig. 4b, Fig. 5b) came out partly scrambled by the conversion. I only report figure values I could map onto labels without ambiguity, using the label order in Fig. S2. Everything else is taken from the running text or from Table S1.
key_findings: Method: VASP, PAW, PBE-D3, 400 eV cutoff, spin-polarised, 5x3 rectangular graphene supercell, k-mesh 3x3x1. Constant-potential DFT: electron count optimised at the target potential, U_SHE = -4.6 - phi/e (VASPsol), converted to RHE at pH 6.8. Barriers come from slow-growth AIMD with a constant-potential hybrid-solvation model (90 explicit H2O, 300 K, H mass 2 amu).
Only Ni was studied, on NiN4, NiN3C, NiN2C2-p, NiN2C2-o1, NiN2C2-o2, NiNC3 and NiC4. All of these are four-coordinate in-plane motifs (Fig. 1a). No O or S donors and no other metals were computed.

Definition: dG*H = dE*H (from CP-DFT total energies) + dZPE - TdS + eU_RHE (CHE). Here dG*H is the free energy of H adsorption on the nonmetal donor atom itself (C or N bound to Ni), not on the metal.

N donors: 'hydrogenation at the N site is thermodynamically highly unfavorable at 0 VRHE for all systems'. dG*H is about 1 eV for NiN4, NiN3C, NiN2C2-o1 and -o2 (heat map at 0 V: NiN4 0.99; NiN3C 0.96/0.92/0.84; NiN2C2-p 0.97/0.96; o1 0.92; o2 1.04 eV). The most favourable N case is NiNC3, still 0.69 eV at 0 V and -0.22 eV only at -1.2 V_RHE, and that step is judged kinetically limited.
C donors in NiNC3: at 0 V_RHE dG*H(C1) = -0.48, C2 = -0.02, C3 = -0.19 eV. C1 reaches -0.60 at -0.4 V, -0.83 at -0.8 V and -1.20 eV at -1.2 V_RHE (text and Table S1).
Multiple hydrogenation of NiNC3: a second H becomes feasible at about -0.8 V_RHE (C2 -0.40, C3 -0.64 eV). A third H (C2) is -0.49 eV at -1.2 V_RHE, so all three C donors can be hydrogenated there.

Mechanism: a Volmer-like step from interfacial water, NC3 + H2O + e- -> NC3-1H_C1 + OH-, with the H coming from H2O dissociation. Barriers (Table S1): 0.78 eV at 0 V (C1); 0.59 at -0.4 V (C1); second H at C3 1.17 eV at -0.4 V; at -0.8 V C1 0.51, C2 0.75, C3 0.55, second H 0.80 (C1,2) and 0.64 (C1,3), third H 1.39 eV; third H at -1.2 V 0.85 eV.
Kinetic judgement in the paper: 0.78 eV is called 'kinetically feasible at room temperature', about 1.2 eV 'unlikely' and 1.39 eV 'strongly hindered'.
BEP fit on the NiNC3 C sites: Ea = 1.17 dG*H + 1.37 (R2 = 0.903).

Origin of the C/N difference: dE*H at C1 is about 1 eV more negative than at N at every potential. The p-band centre is -2.9 to -3.6 eV for C1 and -5.2 to -5.8 eV for N, and both shift down at more negative potential.

Stability: the leaching energy is dG = G(N4-xCxHy) + G(Ni(s)) + 2eU0 - 2eU_RHE - G(NiN4-xCxHy) (the H atoms stay on the empty vacancy). The SI writes U0 as 0.257 V. Bare NiNC3 has the highest leaching energy at every potential. The leaching energy falls as more H are added and becomes negative when all C are hydrogenated. Fig. 4b values could not be extracted reliably.

Bonding: at -0.8 V_RHE the Ni-(N,C) ICOHP is -14.61 eV in bare NiNC3 and -13.01 eV in 2H_C1,3. A new Ni-H interaction adds ICOHP -2.30 eV. The paper reads this as thermodynamic destabilisation combined with possible kinetic stabilisation through Ni-H bonding.

Electronic structure: at -0.8 V the Ni d-band centre shifts from -1.02 to -1.71 eV and the dz2 centre from -0.86 to -1.77 eV upon hydrogenation. U_PZC is 0.07 V_SHE (bare), -0.24 (1H), -0.30 (2H) and -0.51 V_SHE (3H). NO adsorption becomes markedly weaker on hydrogenated NiNC3, and at -1.2 V_RHE the Ni site is sterically blocked (Fig. S9). The paper does not compute H adsorption on Ni (HER dG_H).
answers:
Donors: C donors bound to the metal are hydrogenated under potential (C-H formation on the carbon itself, via H2O + e- -> C-H + OH-). N donors are not: dG*H is about 0.7-1.0 eV at 0 V_RHE, and only NiNC3 reaches -0.22 eV at -1.2 V_RHE, a step that is kinetically limited. O and S donors were not studied, and only Ni was computed, on 4-coordinate NiN4-xCx sites in a 5x3 graphene cell.

Potentials: NiNC3 C1 is already exergonic at 0 V_RHE (-0.48 eV, barrier 0.78 eV). A second H becomes feasible at about -0.8 V and a third at -1.2 V_RHE. In NiN3C and NiN2C2 sites (two or three N plus C) the first C-H is thermoneutral to endergonic at 0 V (-0.01 to +0.44 eV) and becomes exergonic by -0.4 V (-0.08 to -0.37 eV). BEP: Ea = 1.17 dG*H + 1.37.

Implications for Co-N2OC under HER conditions (0 to -0.3 V_RHE): this is our extrapolation, not computed in the paper. The closest analogues are the NiN2C2 and NiN3C sites, where hydrogenating a single C donor at -0.4 V has dG*H between -0.08 and -0.37 eV. Our C donor could therefore be partly hydrogenated thermodynamically in the HER window. The paper's BEP line would give barriers of roughly 0.9-1.4 eV for such sites, which is slow at room temperature. The BEP line was fitted on NiNC3 only, so this is a rough estimate. Nothing in the paper says how an O donor behaves (protonation of M-O); that needs our own test.

Effect of C-H formation:
1. Stability: in the paper it lowers the metal's leaching free energy, which becomes negative when all C are hydrogenated. Our U_diss of +0.51 V for Co-N2OC, computed against an un-hydrogenated vacancy, should therefore be read as an upper bound if the C donor is hydrogenated.
2. dG_H: the paper does not compute H on the metal. It does show that the C donor itself is a competing H site, that the metal d and dz2 centres shift down by about 0.7-0.9 eV, that a Ni-H interaction appears, and that NO binding weakens. A dG_H on the metal computed for the bare site would therefore probably change; the direction for H is not computed.
comparison_note:
1. Different quantity for dG_H: their dG*H is H adsorption on the nonmetal donor (C or N), computed with constant-potential DFT (charged slab, VASPsol, pH 6.8). Their 0 V_RHE point is therefore a charged system at U_SHE of about -0.40 V. Our dG_H is H on the metal from neutral-cell CHE in vacuum. The two numbers cannot be compared directly.

2. The stability framework is equivalent: their leaching energy is dG = -E_f + n e (U0 - U) = n e (U_diss - U). Their vacancy reference keeps the H atoms (N4-xCxHy), while ours is the bare doped vacancy.

3. Caveats on their reference: they combine U0 (an SHE value) with U_RHE at pH 6.8, a mismatch of about 0.4 V unless corrected elsewhere. They also print U0 = 0.257 V, but the tabulated Ni2+/Ni potential is negative (-0.257 V), so the sign should be checked.

4. Scope: only Ni, only N and C donors, no O or S, no SV/DV comparison (all motifs are 4-coordinate), and a different code (VASP/PAW at 400 eV vs our QE/GBRV). Their finding that N donors resist protonation supports our 'N holds the metal well' conclusion. They say nothing about S or O donors.
impact_on_our_claims:
1. Add a caveat to the stability section. E_f and U_diss are computed against an un-hydrogenated vacancy. Under reducing (HER) potentials, C donors bound to the metal can be hydrogenated: for NiN2C2- and NiN3C-type sites, dG*H is about -0.1 to -0.4 eV at -0.4 V_RHE (Li et al., arXiv:2602.04475). C-H formation lowers the metal's leaching free energy. Our U_diss values for C-containing sites (Co-N2OC +0.51 V, Cu-N2C +0.11 V) are therefore optimistic upper bounds under HER conditions.

2. Suggested check: compute dG_H for H on the C donor (and on the O donor, as a protonation test) of Co-N2OC with the same PBE-D3 setup. If either is below about 0 eV at 0 V, recompute E_f and U_diss with the hydrogenated site and the hydrogenated vacancy as reference. Also recompute metal-site dG_H with the C donor hydrogenated.

3. For dG_H screening: report that donor atoms (C) can be competing H sites and that the metal-site dG_H may change after C-H formation; the paper shows a d-band downshift of about 0.7 eV and weaker adsorbate binding.

4. Our N-vs-S/O conclusions are unaffected. The paper supports N donors being resistant to protonation (dG*H about 1 eV at 0 V).

5. No change to the novelty claim (PDB-based transfer).

title: Unraveling the Stability of N-Doped Graphene Supported Single-Atom and Dual-Atom Catalysts From Pourbaix Diagram
source_used: Abstract from PubMed (PMID 41972767), found through Valency search_by_title. Europe PMC lists it as not open access ('Subscription required'), with no PMCID and no preprint on chemRxiv. The Wiley pages (onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/... and /doi/...) returned HTTP 403. I did not read the full text or the SI, so every statement below rests on the abstract only.
key_findings: Systems (abstract): N-doped graphene-supported single-atom catalysts (SAC) and dual-atom catalysts (DAC) of five metals: Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni. The abstract does not state the coordination (M-N4 or another site); that is only implied by 'N-doped graphene'.

Method (abstract): pH- and potential-dependent Gibbs free-energy criteria for leaching. The dissolved-metal speciation includes 'ions, hydroxides, and oxyanions'. The vacancy left behind is modified structurally by binding with H. Pourbaix diagrams are drawn for each catalyst with and without adsorbates.
Adsorbates named in the abstract: *H, *O, *OH, *OOH.
Results (abstract): Co-SAC and Ni-SAC are stable over a wide range of potential and pH. Co-SAC is stabilised further by *H, *OH or *OOH.
Fe-SAC is stable only with *H, *O or *OOH. Mn-SAC is stable only with *O, and only under certain potentials and pH.
Cr-SAC and the Cr-, Mn- and Fe-DACs are unstable under all conditions. DAC stable regions are generally smaller than SAC stable regions.
The abstract gives no numerical values: no stability windows, no dissolution free energies, no H-capping energies.
answers:
Sites: SACs and DACs on N-doped graphene, with metals Cr, Mn, Fe, Co and Ni. The abstract does not say whether the site is M-N4 or something else.

Adsorbates: *H, *O, *OH and *OOH.

How they build the Pourbaix diagram: leaching is written as a pH- and potential-dependent reaction Gibbs energy. The leached metal ends up as the most stable species in solution (ion, hydroxide or oxyanion), not as bulk metal or a single M^n+. The empty vacancy left behind is capped with H. Diagrams are made for the bare sites and for sites carrying adsorbates. The abstract does not give the exact equations, the reference energies, or the number of H atoms used for capping.

Co-N4 at hydrogen-evolution potentials in acid: the abstract says Co-SAC is stable 'over a wide range of potentials and pH' and is stabilised further by *H. That suggests the Co site, likely with *H on it, is stable under acidic HER conditions. The abstract does not explicitly cover pH 0 at U < 0 V(RHE), so this is abstract-based and unconfirmed.

How their criterion compares with ours: ours is U_diss = U0 - E_f/n. It refers to bulk metal, a single ion M^n+ and the bare relaxed empty site, and it ignores adsorbates. Their criterion differs in three ways:
- (a) H capping makes the product side more stable, so their criterion is stricter in acid.
- (b) Hydroxide and oxyanion species make it stricter at high pH.
- (c) Adsorbates on the intact site can make it looser.

My derivation, not from the paper: write the dissolution as M@site + k(H+ + e-) -> site-H_k + M^n+ + n e-. Then ΔG = -E_f + ΔG_cap + k·e·U_RHE + n·e·(U0 - U_SHE), where ΔG_cap = E(site-H_k) - E(site) - (k/2)μ(H2). For k = n the potential term drops out: ΔG = -E_f + ΔG_cap + n(eU0 + 0.059·pH). At pH 0 the site survives only if U_diss > -ΔG_cap/n, and that holds at every potential, HER potentials included. Since ΔG_cap is normally negative, H capping raises the bar our sites have to clear.

Effect on our verdicts:
- Cu-N2C (U_diss +0.11 V) is the most likely to flip to unstable in acid, if |ΔG_cap|/2 > 0.11 eV.
- Co-N2OC (+0.51 V) keeps a margin, but it shrinks by |ΔG_cap|/n.
- Zn-N3 (E_f -0.16 eV, U_diss -0.68 V) stays unstable.
- None of these can be quantified from the abstract.
comparison_note:
The two works measure different things, so they cannot be compared number for number. Our U_diss = U0 - E_f/n uses three references: bulk metal (through E_f), the standard M/M^n+ couple, and the relaxed doped vacancy without H. That makes it a potential threshold for oxidative dissolution at a single, pH-free ion reference.

Their criterion (abstract) uses three different ingredients:
- (1) The most stable dissolved species at each pH and U: ions, hydroxides or oxyanions.
- (2) An H-capped vacancy as the product.
- (3) Adsorbate-covered sites (*H, *O, *OH, *OOH) as the reactant.

H capping turns part of the dissolution into proton-driven, non-faradaic demetalation that depends on pH. As a result, acidic stability can fail even at the low potentials where our U_diss would call a site stable. Adsorbates work the other way and can widen the stable region, for example Co-SAC with *H/*OH/*OOH, and Fe-SAC and Mn-SAC being stable only with adsorbates.

Their qualitative ranking fits our results in part: Co is among the most stable, and our only negative-E_f non-Zn site is Co-N2OC. Their Cr instability fits our observation that E_f follows the bulk cohesive energy. Their sites, however, are N-only on N-doped graphene, with M-N4 presumed but not confirmed in the abstract. They contain no S or O donors and no Cu or Zn, so our donor-chemistry claims (N holds the metal better than S) are not tested by this paper.
impact_on_our_claims:
1. Methods/limitations section: state that U_diss = U0 - E_f/n is a necessary but not sufficient criterion. It leaves out three things:
   - (a) Protonation/H capping of the emptied vacancy, which causes acid demetalation that is independent of potential.
   - (b) Hydroxide and oxyanion dissolution products at higher pH.
   - (c) Stabilisation of the intact site by adsorbates.
   Cite Meng and Zhong 2026 for the full pH-potential treatment.

2. Optional low-cost extension: for the three borderline sites (Co-N2OC, Cu-N2C, Zn-N3), relax the empty doped vacancy capped with k H atoms (k = n, one H on each N/O donor or dangling C). Then evaluate ΔG(pH) = -E_f + ΔG_cap + n(eU0 + 0.059 pH), with ΔG_cap = E(site-H_k) - E(site) - (k/2)μ(H2) including ZPE-TS corrections. Report whether Cu-N2C (+0.11 V) and Co-N2OC (+0.51 V) still pass at pH 0.

3. Soften the verdict wording. Write 'passes the bulk-metal/ion dissolution criterion' instead of 'stable under operating conditions'.

4. Leave the novelty claim unchanged. This paper screens N-only SAC/DAC Pourbaix stability for Cr to Ni and does not transfer enzyme first shells.
